gap: None of the results ChatGPT got works out how much of a dock's 'laptop charging' its own power brick actually supplies. The AV Access KD-E10 lists '100 W' PD, but its brick is 12 V × 3 A = 36 W, the dock itself can draw up to 33.12 W, and AV Access says to plug in the laptop's original adapter as well. That leaves the laptop 0 W from the KD-E10's own brick. The iDock M10's brick is 20 V × 6 A = 120 W, which covers its 100 W PD and leaves 20 W for the dock.
standout_why: I compared four pages. Racks & Watts (cited) gives the iDock C10 as 'up to 60 W' and says itself that it doesn't know how much power reaches the laptop. TESmart's 2026 buying guide (cited) gives only '100W PD' for the HDC203-PM24, with no adapter rating and no net figure. The Office Journal's laptop+desktop list gives 65 W for the iDock P10 and only says to 'verify the budget is shared'. ChatGPT's answer says 'up to 100W laptop charging' for the T722. None of these compares a brick's rating with the PD figure, and none notes that one '100 W' dock is only a pass-through for the laptop's own charger.
decides: This supports the iDock M10 over the KD-E10 for anyone who wants to plug in one cable and leave their laptop charger in the bag. The M10's own 120 W brick covers 100 W PD, and on M4/M5 or Pro/Max Macs it runs two extended screens, which works out to $289.99 / 2 = $145 per extended screen. The KD-E10 at $169.99 still makes sense for a Windows laptop if the shopper keeps their laptop charger at the desk anyway. Our own table should change its KD-E10 'Laptop charging: 100 W' cell to '100 W pass-through (needs your laptop charger)'. The iDock C10 supplies 60 W from its own brick. That is 60 / 140 = 43% of a 140 W MacBook Pro charger's rating, and AV Access itself sends 140 W laptops to the KD-E10 or the original adapter.
